verse.text: The elder, to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.
Beloved, I pray that in every respect it may go well with you and that you may be in good health, just as it goes well with your soul.
verse.note: The verb can mean either 'pray' or simply 'wish'. A wish for the recipient's health was a standard opening in Greek letters of the period, so a first-century reader would hear a familiar courtesy here, given a Christian turn by the reference to the soul. The verse is a conventional greeting, not a promise of prosperity.

verse.text: For I rejoiced greatly when brothers came and testified to your truth, to how you are walking in truth.
I have no greater joy than this, to hear that my children are walking in the truth.
Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers, strangers though they are.
They have testified to your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God,
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, or in the Greek Old Testament Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word, though it can sound like a one-off meeting.

note.traditional: send them on their journey / bring forward on their journey

verse.note: In early Christian usage this verb was close to a technical term for equipping travellers for the next stage of a journey with food, money and sometimes companions. Gaius is being asked for practical support, not merely a farewell.

verse.text: for they set out for the sake of the Name, taking nothing from the pagans.

note.traditional: his name's sake / the sake of the Name

verse.note: The Greek says only 'the name' without saying whose. Most interpreters take it as the name of Jesus, as elsewhere in early Christian speech about missionaries; others hear the Jewish reverential use of 'the Name' for God. The Greek does not decide between them.

The word means 'people of the nations', that is, those outside God's people. Many versions translate 'Gentiles', but Gaius and his circle bear Greek names and were probably non-Jews themselves, so the contrast is with unbelievers, not with an ethnic group. The point is that the travelling brothers did not take support from those they were evangelising. Some versions accordingly have 'pagans' or 'non-believers'.

verse.text: So we ought to take such people in, so that we may become co-workers with the truth.
verse.note: The Greek can mean working together with the truth, the truth being pictured as itself active (as in verse 12, where it testifies), or working together with the missionaries for the truth. Translations and commentators are divided, and either reading fits the context.

verse.text: I wrote something to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not receive us.

note.traditional: receiveth us not / does not acknowledge our authority

verse.note: The same verb is used in verse 10 for refusing hospitality to the travelling brothers, and it is rendered the same way in both places. Here it may mean that Diotrephes refuses to welcome the elder's emissaries, or more broadly that he does not accept the elder's authority; many versions choose the second. 'Us' may refer to the elder alone or to him and his associates.

verse.text: For this reason, if I come, I will bring up the things he is doing, spouting malicious nonsense about us. And not content with that, he does not receive the brothers himself, and those who want to he stops and throws out of the assembly.
Beloved, do not imitate what is evil but what is good. The one who does good is from God; the one who does evil has not seen God.
Everyone testifies in Demetrius’s favor, and so does the truth itself. We testify too, and you know that our testimony is true.

note.traditional: Demetrius hath good report of all men

verse.note: This verse follows the form of an ancient letter of recommendation. Demetrius was probably the bearer of the letter and one of the travelling brothers whom Gaius is being asked to welcome, though the letter does not say so explicitly.

verse.text: I had many things to write to you, but I do not want to write to you with ink and pen.
I hope to see you soon, and we will speak face to face.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'mouth to mouth', a Semitic idiom found in the Greek Old Testament for direct personal speech. 'Face to face' is the English equivalent; the literal phrase would mislead a modern reader.

verse.text: Peace to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.
verse.note: Verse numbering differs between editions here. Some English Bibles, including the King James Version, print these closing greetings as the end of verse 14 and have no verse 15. The wording is not affected.
